source_text: ᾿Ἐξαιτοῦμαι δὲ παρά τε φιλοσόφων τῶν νῦν ὄντων, σοὺυς αὐτὸς ἔγνων καὶ ὃσους ἄλλων διηγουμένων ἤκουσα, καὶ παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἀνθρώπων, ἀνεμεσήτως ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ νῦν ἡμῖν λεγόμενα. μηδέ μέ τις ἢ φιλίᾳ τῇ πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα ἢ καὶ ἀπτεχϑανόμενον ἔτι τοῖς λοιποῖς φιλοσόφοις (ὧν, εἴπτερ τις ἄλλος, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐραστής ve διὰ τοὺς λόγους εἶναι ϑέλω, καὶ εὐφημεῖν αὐτοὺς βούλομαι αὐτός τε καὶ ἑτέρων τὰ κάλλιστα λεγόντων περὶ αὐτῶν ἀκούεξιν᾽ ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοιαῦτά ἐστιν, ὡς εἰς ἔσχατον περιϊβρίζεσϑαι μὲν ὑπὸ πάντων σχεδὸν καὶ τοὔνομα τῆς φιλοσοφίας, ἐμὲ δὲ μικροῦ δεῖν ἰδιωτεύειν ἑλέσϑαι πτάντη, ἤπερ τι μαϑεῖν ὧν οὗτοι ἀπαγγέλλουσιν, οἷς διὰ τὸν λοιττὸν βίον οὐδὲ προσιέναι ἄξιον εἶναι ἐδόκουν, ἴσως οὐκ ὀρϑῶς τοῦτο φρονῶν), πλὴν μή μέ τις φιλοτιμίᾳ τινὶ ἤτοι τῶν εἰς τὸν ἄνδρα ἐπαίνων ἢ τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ἔξω φιλοσόφους ἄλλῃ ταύτῃ φιλο- τὸ τιμίᾳ ταῦτα λέγειν ὑπονοησάτω" ἀλλὰ καὶ μικρότερα ἡμᾶς τῶν αὐτοῖ: ἔργων, μὴ κολακεύειν δοχοίημεν, λέγειν τεεττείσϑω οὐχὲ ῥήματα καὶ ὀνόματα καὶ ἀφορμὰς ἐντέχνους ἐγχωμίων ἑαυτοῖς ἐχποριζομένοις" ὃς οὐδ᾽ ὕτε μειράκιον ὧν τὴν δημώδη ῥητορικὴν ἔχ. ῥήτορος ἐδιδασκόμην, ἐπαινεῖν καὶ τὸ λέγειν περί του ἐγκώμιον, ὃ τι μὴ ἀληϑὲς ἦν, ἑκὼν ὑπέμενον. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ νῦν ἐπαινεῖν ττροϑέμενος, ἁπλῶς τοῖς ἑτέρων ψόγοις τοῦτον ἐξαίρειν οἶμαι δεῖν" ἢ κακῶς ἂν ἔλεγον τὸν ἄνδρα, τοῖς ἄλλων πταίσμασιν, ἵνα τι ττερὶ αὐτοῦ μεῖζον δὴ λέγειν ἔχοιμι, τταραβαλὼν τὸν μακάριον αὐτοῦ βίον" οὐχ οὕτως ἀφραίνομεν᾽ ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸ ὃ πέπονθα δίχα τινὸς παραβολῆς χαὶ τεανουργίας τῆς ἐν λόγοις ὁμολογήσω.
pass_a_gloss: I demand from both the philosophers who are now and whom I myself know and as many as I have heard from others telling, and from the other people, to have without partiality towards the things now being said to us. Let no one either because of friendship towards the man or even still being dependent on the other philosophers (whom, if someone else, and I myself also being a lover of them because of the words wish to be, and I want to speak well of them, and I am pleased when others speaking the best things about them hear) but for these are such that they are almost despised by all and the name of philosophy is brought to an end, and I am about to choose to be a private person rather than to learn anything of what these announce, to whom because of their rest of life it did not seem worthy to approach, perhaps not thinking this correctly) except let no one suppose that I say these things because of some ambition either of the praises towards the man or of the other ambition towards the external philosophers. But also let us not seem to flatter, saying lesser things than their deeds, and let us not speak empty words and names and clever expressions, which they provide for themselves. For I, not even when I was a young man, when I was being taught the common rhetoric of a rhetorician, endured willingly to praise and to say an encomium about something which was not true. So then not even now, being about to praise, do I think it is necessary to extol him simply by the censures of others, or to speak badly about the man because of the faults of others, so that I might have something greater to say about him, by comparing his blessed life. We do not think in this way; but I will acknowledge what I have experienced, without any comparison and fabrication of words.

choices.why: it is an adverb indicating impartiality
it is a noun indicating a person who loves or is fond of something
it is a verb indicating to speak favorably of someone or something

pass_b_english: I ask both the philosophers living today — those I know personally and those I have heard about from others — and everyone else to listen to what I am saying now without bias. Let no one think I speak this way because of friendship toward the man, or because I still depend on the other philosophers (I want to be, if anyone else is, a lover of them because of their words; I want to speak well of them and I am glad when I hear others speaking well of them). But these things are such that philosophy is almost despised by everyone and its very name is brought to an end, and I was about to choose to be a private person rather than learn anything from what these men proclaim — men to whom, because of the rest of their lives, it did not seem worthy to approach, perhaps not thinking this correctly). Let no one suppose that I say these things out of some ambition, either from praise toward the man or from another kind of ambition toward the outside philosophers. But also let us not seem to flatter by saying lesser things than their deeds deserve, and let us not speak empty words and names and clever expressions which they provide for themselves. For I, not even when I was a young man learning the common rhetoric of a rhetorician, endured willingly to praise or to give an encomium about something that was not true. So then not even now, when I am about to praise, do I think it necessary to extol him simply by the censures of others, or to speak badly of the man because of the faults of others so that I might have something greater to say about him by comparing his blessed life. We do not think in this way; but I will acknowledge what I have experienced, without any comparison or fabrication of words.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex syntax of the Greek, particularly the parenthetical section regarding the author's affection for philosophers. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source. The title 'Against Mere Word-Sages' captures the essence of the critique of 'clever expressions' and 'empty words'.
